userJob: Present a set of capabilities without the row of three identical cards
problem: Three features become three equal cards in a row, which is the single most recognisable machine-built section on the web and encodes that all three matter equally when they do not
worksWhen: Recognising the pattern in your own draft, or in an existing page during a redesign audit
avoidWhen: The three items genuinely are equal and interchangeable, and the brief asked for a comparison of equals
mechanism: NO 3-column equal feature cards. The generic "three identical cards horizontally" feature row is banned. Use 2-column zig-zag, asymmetric grid, scroll-pinned, or horizontal-scroll alternative.
risks: Replacing three equal cards with four equal cards, which is the same claim with one more column
Choosing the alternative by preference rather than by which item actually carries most weight
mobileRules: All three collapse to one column at 375px, where the equality claim disappears and the source order becomes the hierarchy; decide that order deliberately
accessibilityRules: If the cards are links, each is one focusable target with an accessible name that is not just the heading repeated
genericnessNote: This is the reference case for machine-built layout, and its named alternatives are themselves converging, so the composition still has to follow from the content's real weights.

userJob: Show a product interface without building a fake one out of rectangles
problem: A hero needs a product visual and none exists, so a fake dashboard, task list or terminal is assembled from styled containers, and it is the most recognisable machine-design tell there is
worksWhen: Any page that wants to show software it cannot photograph
avoidWhen: A real, running component preview embedded in the page, which is the actual product rather than a picture of it
mechanism: NO div-based fake screenshots. Never build a fake product UI out of `<div>` rectangles to simulate a screenshot. Use real images, generated images, or skip the preview.
risks: Adding fake version strings and timestamps inside the fake preview, which compounds the tell
Skipping the preview and leaving a dead field where it was, which fails the first-screen check instead
mobileRules: A fake preview is usually illegible at 375px, which is where the pretence is easiest to see
accessibilityRules: A fake interface built from containers is announced as a pile of unlabelled text to a screen reader
If a real screenshot is used, its alt text says what the screen is showing, not that it is a screenshot
genericnessNote: The fake preview is the default answer to a missing asset, so it appears on unrelated products in near-identical form.

userJob: Label a section without enumerating it
problem: Every section gets a small numbered label above its heading, which claims the content is an ordered sequence when it is a set, and produces the same rhythm on every page
worksWhen: Reviewing your own section headers, or auditing an existing page
avoidWhen: The content genuinely is numbered and the reader needs the number, such as steps in a procedure they will follow out of order
mechanism: NO section-number eyebrows. `00 / INDEX`, `001 · Capabilities`, `002 · Featured commission`, `06 · how it works`, `05 · The honest table` - banned. Eyebrows should name the topic in plain language, not enumerate.
risks: Keeping the eyebrow and dropping only the number, which leaves the templated rhythm intact
Numbering a set to make it look ordered, which is a structural claim with nothing behind it
mobileRules: At 375px the numbered label often takes a whole line above the heading, spending vertical space on nothing
accessibilityRules: A decorative eyebrow inside the heading element is read out as part of the heading, so keep it outside or hide it from assistive technology
genericnessNote: Numbering is the cheapest available way to look structured, which is exactly why it appears on unrelated pages in identical form.

userJob: End the first screen without telling the reader to scroll
problem: A scroll label or animated wheel icon is placed at the bottom of the hero, which tells a reader who has not scrolled yet something they already know
avoidWhen: A page where scrolling is genuinely non-obvious because the first screen is a full-height interactive canvas that captures the wheel
mechanism: Scroll cues are banned. `Scroll`, `↓ scroll`, `Scroll to explore`, `Scroll to walk through it`, animated mouse-wheel icons. If the user has not scrolled yet, they are looking at the hero. They know what scroll is. The bottom of the viewport does not need a label.
risks: Replacing the label with a decorative arrow, which is the same cue with fewer words
Using the cue to fill a dead field at the bottom of the hero, which is a composition problem the cue hides
mobileRules: At 375px the cue occupies space the first screen needs for the object that owns it
accessibilityRules: An animated cue is motion with no meaning, so it is removed under reduced motion rather than slowed
genericnessNote: The cue is furniture rather than a look, but its presence is a reliable marker that the first screen was not composed.

userJob: Separate rows in a long list without ruling all of them
problem: A ten-row specification gets a rule above and below every row, so the page is a ladder of hairlines and the grouping carries no information
worksWhen: Any list, specification or comparison longer than a few rows
avoidWhen: A dense operating listing an operator scans daily, where consistent row rules are what makes scanning possible
mechanism: NO `border-t` + `border-b` on every row of a long list / spec table. Pick one (bottom-border between rows OR top-border above the group) and use it sparsely.
risks: Removing the rules and leaving rows with no grouping at all, which is harder to read than the ladder
Replacing rules with cards, which turns ten hairlines into ten containers
mobileRules: At 375px rows usually become stacked pairs, where a rule between every value and its label is worse than at desktop
accessibilityRules: Grouping by rule is visual only; the underlying structure still needs real table or definition list semantics
genericnessNote: Hairline separators recur across unrelated trades for honest reasons, so this is a signal to read rather than a rule to enforce blindly.

userJob: Separate items in a metadata line without a chain of middle dots
problem: A metadata strip becomes a run of values joined by middle dots, which is used as the default separator for everything and reads as decoration rather than structure
worksWhen: Any metadata line, caption, byline or footer strip
avoidWhen: A single separator between exactly two values, which is what the character is for
mechanism: The middle-dot (`·`) is rationed. Maximum 1 per line in metadata strips. Do NOT use it as the default separator for everything ("foo · bar · baz · qux · quux"). If you need a separator family, prefer line breaks, hairlines, or columns.
risks: Swapping the middle dot for a slash or a pipe, which is the same chain in another glyph
Using the strip to carry values that deserve their own line
mobileRules: A dotted chain wraps unpredictably at 375px, breaking between a value and its separator
accessibilityRules: A separator character is read out by some screen readers, so a chain of them becomes noise in the announcement
genericnessNote: The chain is a habit rather than a look, but it is a reliable marker of a metadata line nobody designed.

userJob: Punctuate without the long dash that marks machine-written copy
problem: The long dash is the most reliable stylistic marker of generated text, and softer wording such as use it sparingly has failed repeatedly in practice
worksWhen: Every visible string: headlines, eyebrows, pills, body copy, quotes, attribution, captions, button text and alt text
avoidWhen: Never; the rule is binary rather than a limit
mechanism: Zero long dashes anywhere the user can see, in either the long or the short form when used as a separator. Restructure instead: two sentences with a full stop, a comma, parentheses, or a colon. Ranges use a plain hyphen. The only dash characters permitted are the plain hyphen and the minus sign in mathematics.
risks: Allowing it in body copy because it reads naturally there, which is how the limit failed before
Checking the rendered page but not alt text, button labels and error strings
accessibilityRules: Screen readers treat the character inconsistently, so a sentence built around it can be announced without its pause
genericnessNote: Punctuation is not a look, but this one character is the most reliable single tell there is.

userJob: Choose sample values that do not read as invented
problem: Placeholder data is written as round or maximally clean figures, so a page of real-looking evidence is filled with values no real system would produce
worksWhen: Any placeholder data, sample dashboard, example record or demonstration figure
avoidWhen: The figure is real, where its roundness is a fact rather than a choice
mechanism: NO fake-perfect numbers. Avoid `99.99%`, `50%`, `1234567`. Use organic, messy data (`47.2%`, `+1 (312) 847-1928`).
risks: Replacing round invented numbers with precise invented numbers, which is a worse claim rather than a better one
Leaving sample data unmarked, so a reader takes it for the client's real figures
mobileRules: Messy figures are longer, so check that a column of them does not wrap at 375px
accessibilityRules: Sample data is labelled as sample in text, not only in a code comment, so it is announced as such
genericnessNote: The tell is the shape of the number rather than its value, and the same invented shapes recur across unrelated products.

userJob: Label a testimonial, journal or sidebar section in plain language
problem: Section labels reach for poetic phrasing such as field notes or on our desks, which reads as performed craftsmanship and appears on unrelated sites in nearly identical form
worksWhen: Any label above a quote, blog, sidebar or activity section
avoidWhen: The phrase is the client's own established term for the thing, which makes it their vocabulary rather than yours
mechanism: NO "From the field" / "Field notes" / "Currently on the bench" / "On our desks" / "Loose plates" style poetic labels on quote, blog, or sidebar sections. Reads as performative-craftsman. Use plain functional labels ("Testimonials", "Latest writing", "Now working on") or skip the label.
risks: Inventing a new poetic label rather than dropping the label, which moves the tell one word along
Dropping the label from a section that genuinely needed a heading for navigation
mobileRules: A dropped label frees a line at 375px, which is usually the right trade
accessibilityRules: A section that loses its visible label still needs an accessible name if it is a landmark
genericnessNote: These labels are drawn from a shared and small vocabulary, so two unrelated sites reach the same phrase independently.

userJob: Choose a dark ground that is not the maximum value
problem: Dark mode defaults to the absolute black value, which produces harsh edges against light type and gives the palette no room below its darkest surface
worksWhen: Any dark scheme, and any dark section within a light page
avoidWhen: The material genuinely is that value, for example an OLED-first product or a brief that names it
mechanism: NO pure black (`#000000`). Off-black, zinc-950, or charcoal.
risks: Choosing an off-black with a hue that fights the palette's own temperature
Fixing the ground and leaving pure white type on it, which keeps the harshness
mobileRules: Check the contrast against the same off-black at 375px, where the type sizes are smaller
accessibilityRules: Body text still needs 4.5:1 against the chosen ground, which an off-black makes slightly harder rather than easier
Measure the dark scheme independently; a light-mode pass proves nothing about it
genericnessNote: Avoiding the maximum value is a calibration rather than a style, but the two or three off-blacks everyone reaches for are themselves a default.

userJob: Recognise the whole cluster of defaults rather than one of them at a time
problem: Each default is avoided individually while the overall combination still lands, because the interface face, the gradient family and the layout habits arrive together
worksWhen: As a final read of a finished page, after the individual checks have passed
avoidWhen: As a substitute for the individual checks, which it is not specific enough to replace
mechanism: NEVER use generic AI-generated aesthetics like overused font families (Inter, Roboto, Arial, system fonts), cliched color schemes (particularly purple gradients on white backgrounds), predictable layouts and component patterns, and cookie-cutter design that lacks context-specific character.
risks: Treating the named items as the whole list, so the next unnamed default passes
Reacting by adding decoration, which produces a busier page with the same underlying structure
mobileRules: The cluster is more visible at 375px, where the layout habits collapse into the same single column everywhere
accessibilityRules: Escaping the default palette does not exempt the replacement from contrast measurement; new palettes fail more often than familiar ones
genericnessNote: This post names the failure mode the whole package exists to prevent, and naming defaults only moves the work to the next unnamed one.
